note: Source rules and cautions are reworded as short sentences. Their figures and thresholds are unchanged.

rule_groups.title: Solar power
paragraphs: Each class is a rough estimate by our own rule. It is not a measurement or an engineering study.
The daily panel yield for each kilowatt of panels is the daily sunlight on level ground, in kWh per square metre, multiplied by 0.75.
The rating of a panel assumes 1 kW of sunlight per square metre. The factor 0.75 includes the losses from heat, dirt, snow, wires and the inverter.
Panels that are tilted toward a low Sun can give more power. This estimate does not include that increase.
If the yearly mean is at least 4.5 kWh per square metre per day, solar is good. That is approximately 1,640 kWh per square metre in a year.
Solar is fair from 3.0 up to 4.5 kWh per square metre per day. Solar is poor below 3.0.
These cut values are our own. Sunny deserts usually give 5.5 to 7 kWh per square metre per day.
Central Europe gives approximately 3 kWh per square metre per day. The high Arctic gives approximately 2.
A month has no Sun only if NASA POWER gives exactly 0.0 for it. If a month is blank, it is unknown, not dark.
The yearly mean is the simple mean of the 12 monthly means. It includes direct and diffuse sunlight.
Sunlight comes from NASA POWER ALLSKY_SFC_SW_DWN and CERES SYN1deg. The monthly means are for the years of the service and for the 1-degree box that contains the area.

rule_groups.title: A panel that faces a low Sun
paragraphs: Above the air, the sunlight is 1,361 watts per square metre at Earth and at the Moon. This value comes from the NASA NSSDCA fact sheets.
On the Moon, a vertical panel that faces a Sun on the horizon gets all of that beam. There is no air to make it less bright.
Air mass is the thickness of air that the sunlight goes through, compared with a Sun directly overhead. The Sun height h is in degrees.
The formula for sea level is AM = 1 / (sin h + 0.50572 × (h + 6.07995)^−1.6364). It does not include the height of the area.
The air-mass formula is from Applied Optics 28(22), 4735–4738 (1989).
Clear-air direct beam = 1,361 × 0.7^(AM^0.678) watts per square metre. The panel faces the Sun.
This formula comes from Applied Solar Energy (1976), as PVEducation quotes it. In typical clear air, 0.7 of the sunlight goes through one air mass.
The exponent 0.678 allows for air that is not uniform.
The Sun ceilings of the lunar regions are 2.08, 5.55, 6.11 and 7.59 degrees. We calculate the power at each ceiling and at half of that height.
During many of the hours of low Sun, the Sun is below its ceiling.
For each best ten-day period, the clear share is 1 − cloud percent / 100. We give each period a weight by its hours of low Sun.
We calculate the mean of those shares over the months of the best periods. The periods come from the low-Sun data for each lunar region.
The cloud figures are CERES SYN1deg monthly means over all hours. The low-Sun power under a typical sky is the clear-air power multiplied by that clear share.
If the cloud is unknown, the figure for a typical sky is unknown. It is also unknown if the area has no best periods for that lunar region.

rule_groups.title: Wind power
paragraphs: Each class is a rough estimate by our own rule.
The standard air density at sea level is 1.225 kilograms per cubic metre. We use the International Standard Atmosphere.
For height z metres in the lower 11 km, density = 1.225 × (1 − 0.0065 × z / 288.15)^4.2559.
The height z is the mean height of the model box that holds the 50 m wind. If there is no height, we use the density at sea level.
If the height of the model box is unknown, it stays unknown. Cold polar air can be approximately 10% denser at −15 °C. The figure does not include this increase.
For the usual spread of wind speeds, the mean of the speed cubed is 6 / pi times the mean speed cubed. Rounded, this factor is 1.91.
Power in wind at 50 m = 0.5 × air density × 1.91 × (yearly mean speed)^3. The units are watts per square metre of rotor area.
This is the power that the wind carries. A turbine takes a maximum of 59%, and in practice 35% to 45%.
The yearly speed is the simple mean of the 12 monthly means of NASA POWER WS50M. These means come from the MERRA-2 reanalysis.
The nearest MERRA-2 point is for a grid box of 0.5 by 0.625 degrees. The monthly means of wind include all hours.
Wind classes at 50 m come from the US Department of Energy and NREL atlas (1986).
Class 1 is below 200 watts per square metre. Classes 2, 3 and 4 start at 200, 300 and 400.
Classes 5, 6 and 7 start at 500, 600 and 800 watts per square metre.
At sea level, those boundaries match mean speeds of 5.6, 6.4, 7.0, 7.5, 8.0 and 8.8 m/s.
These bands follow the published table as the author of the source knows it. Nobody saved a copy of the table with these inputs.
Wind is good in class 4 and higher, at 400 watts per square metre or more. It is fair in classes 2 and 3.
Fair is from 200 up to 400 watts per square metre. Wind is poor in class 1, below 200.

rule_groups.title: Geothermal power
paragraphs: Each class is a rough estimate by our own rule.
Geothermal is good if an active geothermal power plant is within 50 km. A volcano within 30 km that erupted in 1990 or later also gives this class.
The plants come from the WRI Global Power Plant Database. Their primary fuel must be geothermal.
A recent volcano has a listed year of last eruption of 1990 or later. A confirmed eruption that started or stopped in 1990 or later also makes a volcano recent.
Geothermal is fair if an active plant is within 150 km. A Holocene volcano within 100 km also gives this class.
Holocene means the last 11,700 years. In all other conditions, geothermal is poor.
Volcanoes and eruptions come from the Smithsonian Global Volcanism Program.

rule_groups.title: Volcanic influences
paragraphs: Each class is a rough estimate by our own rule.
Steady volcanic effects are likely if a volcano that agrees with the next rule is within 30 km of the centre of the area.
That volcano must have eruptions in 3 or more separate years from 1990, or an eruption in 2015 or later.
Volcanic effects come and go if a volcano that erupted in 1990 or later is within 100 km. In all other conditions, we expect no volcanic effects.
Possible effects are gas and volcanic haze that can corrode instruments and optics, and make optics less clear. Fine ash and abrasive dust can be on the ground and in the air.
Warm ground or steam can change temperature measurements. Small volcanic tremors, and closure of the area during eruptions, can also affect the work.
For young volcanic ground, a Holocene volcano within 50 km and volcanic rock on the rock map are necessary. Holocene means active in approximately the last 11,700 years.
It is false if no Holocene volcano is that near, or if the rock map shows rock that is not volcanic. It is unknown if a volcano is that near but the rock map gives no class.
Fresh lava and ash can represent the basalt soil of the dark plains of the Moon and of Mars.

rule_groups.title: Human influences
paragraphs: Each class is a rough estimate by our own rule.
Steady human disturbance is likely if one of these conditions is true. One condition is a listed settlement of 1,000 people or more within 5 km.
A main road or railway within 2 km also gives this class. An airfield with scheduled flights within 10 km also gives this class.
Human disturbance is possible if a listed settlement of any size is within 25 km. A main road, a railway or an airfield of any type within 10 km also gives this class.
Otherwise, the area is undisturbed as far as our lists show.
Possible effects are vibration from vehicles and aircraft, radio noise, dust from traffic and artificial light. Tracks and litter can be in camera views.
Help is within reach if a listed settlement of 1,000 people or more is within 50 km.
An airfield with scheduled flights within 100 km also gives this result. Help means possible power, shelter and rescue. In all other conditions, this flag is false.
The nearest listed settlement comes from GeoNames cities1000. If there is no population figure, the population stays unknown.
The population within 25 km is the sum of the listed populations. If no settlement is listed, it is zero.
It is unknown if there are settlements but none has a population figure. If only some figures are not available, the sum is a lower bound.
Roads and railways come from Natural Earth 1:10m, without ferries. If there is no road or railway within 1,000 km, the distance is unknown.
Airfields come from the OurAirports list of runway airports of all sizes, with gravel and ice strips. The list does not include heliports, seaplane bases or closed fields.
Scheduled flights come from a flag in the airfield list. The points on a road are a maximum of 1.5 km apart. Thus, a distance to a road can be too large by a maximum of 0.75 km.
The simplified road lines can be a kilometre or more away from the real roads.

rule_groups.title: Our small-tremor estimate
paragraphs: Each class is a rough estimate by our own rule. If the earthquake catalogue can give a verdict, we use that verdict.
Small tremors are likely if a volcano that erupted in 1990 or later is within 50 km.
At least 5 earthquakes of magnitude 5 or more within 200 km from 1990 also give this class.
Small tremors are possible if a Holocene volcano of any date is within 100 km.
Between 1 and 4 earthquakes of magnitude 5 or more within 200 km from 1990 also give this class.
Glacier ice on 10% or more of the land of the area also gives this class. Ice that moves makes small quakes.
In all other conditions, small tremors are unlikely. If the earthquake input or the glacier input is not available, the class stays unknown.
The input for larger earthquakes covers 1990–2025. Glacier ice comes from ESA WorldCover in the north and from the share of ice sheet in the south.
We keep our estimate also where the catalogue sees small tremors. Thus, you can compare the two.

rule_groups.title: The earthquake catalogue verdict
paragraphs: Each class is a rough estimate by our own rule. It is not an engineering standard.
The USGS catalogue covers 2010–2025, a period of 16 years. The events have a magnitude of 1 or more and less than 5.
We count all types of magnitude and all types of event. Earthquakes, quarry blasts, explosions and ice quakes can all shake instruments.
For steady small tremors, events within 100 km are necessary in at least 12 of the 16 years. The rate must also be 5 or more per year.
Occasional small tremors means that there is at least one event within 100 km, but the two conditions for steady tremors are not both true.
Thus, there are events in 1 to 11 years, or fewer than 5 per year. Events in 1 to 3 years are usually one swarm.
None recorded applies if the catalogue records small tremors here but shows none within 100 km.
Cannot tell applies if the catalogue cannot see small tremors here.
It also applies if the catalogue sees only magnitudes above a floor between 2.5 and 3.5, and shows no event within 100 km.
In that condition, an empty circle does not tell you about smaller tremors.
The detection floor is the 10th percentile of the magnitudes of the events within 500 km over the 16 years. If there are fewer than 30 events, the floor is unknown.
If the floor is 2.5 or less, the catalogue records small tremors. If the floor is above 2.5 and not more than 3.5, the catalogue records only larger tremors.
If the floor is above 3.5, or if there are too few events, the catalogue cannot see small tremors.
A floor of 2.5 or less must also pass a check near the area. The catalogue must show at least one event below that floor within 200 km.
If not, a better network farther away gave the low floor. Then we treat the area as a place where the catalogue cannot see small tremors.
Examples are western Alaska, seen from Chukotka, and Texas, seen from Coahuila.
Where the catalogue cannot see small tremors, their counts are unknown, never zero. If there is no record, there can still be tremors.
If the catalogue still lists larger events within 100 km, they show some activity. Their count is a lower bound, never a rate of small tremors.
If two catalogue requests give the same event, we keep it only one time, by its event ID.
The requests cover the latitudes from 55 to 90 degrees in each hemisphere. In the north, each request covers one month. In the south, each request covers one year.
If an answer has more than 20,000 events, we request it again by month, then by halves of longitude.

rule_groups.title: Distances, unknown values and data collection
paragraphs: Distances go from the centre of the area along a great circle. The source uses a sphere for the Earth, with a radius of 6,371.0088 km.
Areas are approximately 11 km wide. A point in the area can be approximately 8 km nearer or farther than the distance from the centre.
The data stores unknown as null, never as zero. A count of zero means that the list has no entries in the stated radius.
The search for the nearest feature goes farther until it finds a match. For roads and railways, the search stops at 1,000 km.
The collection of the source data sends one request at a time to NASA POWER, with at least 2 seconds between requests.
After a refusal (429) or a server fault (5xx), the collection waits for at least one minute.
After a lost connection, the collection waits 20, 40, 60 seconds and more, to a maximum of 300 seconds. Then it tries again.
These are the rules for the collection of the source data. This page reads only its local exported data.

solar: This is not a measurement at the area. It is not the yield of a tilted panel, or of a panel that follows the Sun.
It includes the daylight outside the hours of low Sun. At these latitudes, the coarse box is approximately 111 km by 20 to 55 km.
low_sun: This is a textbook estimate for clear air, not a measurement. It does not include diffuse light from the sky.
Real polar air changes with haze, ice crystals and aerosols. A real panel can get less power, or a little more.
The cloud figure is a monthly mean over all hours, not only the hours of low Sun. Its box is approximately 111 km from north to south.
On Earth, the low Sun gives only a part of the power that a panel gets under the same low Sun on the Moon.
On the Moon, no air stops the light.
wind: This is a mean for a coarse grid box, not a measurement at the area. The box is approximately 55 km by 20 to 35 km.
Hills, coasts, valleys, cold winds that flow down from ice, and ice on the blades can change the conditions very much. This is not the power that a turbine gives.
geothermal: Nobody drilled here or measured the heat here. This only shows that hot rock is possibly near the surface.
Areas far from volcanoes can have useful warm ground, for example deep basins and hot springs. Areas near volcanoes can have ground that is not usable.
The source did not get an open world map of geothermal potential, because a login was necessary. The list of plants stops at approximately 2021 and does not include some plants.
volcanic: This is not a hazard map or a forecast of eruptions. One point at the summit or at the centre of the field represents each volcano.
A fissure system or a volcanic field can go far beyond that point. Gas and ash can move with the wind much farther than 100 km.
The years with eruptions are the calendar years in which a confirmed eruption continued. If an eruption has no end year, we count only its start year.
We do not include uncertain or discredited eruptions. We do not count lava lakes or steady gas release between listed eruptions.
A volcano can steam and smell for decades between listed eruptions.
human: This is not a population map, and it is not a measurement of noise or light. Distances are straight-line distances, not travel distances.
GeoNames cities1000 lists settlements of more than 1,000 people and seats of local government. Camps, stations, mines and hamlets are possibly not in the list.
Natural Earth lists only main roads and railways. Most tracks, winter roads and mine roads are not in it.
If the list shows no road, there can still be a road. We know that each airfield exists, but we do not know its traffic.
small_tremors: Our estimate is not a count or a measurement of tremors. It is a guess from active volcanoes, larger earthquakes and glaciers that move.
Small tremors can occur where our estimate says unlikely. Where it says likely, they possibly do not occur.
catalogue: These are catalogued events, not measurements of ground motion at the area. This is not a hazard map. Only a seismometer at the place gives a real test.
The catalogue contains only the events that nearby instruments detect. In Alaska, it records magnitude 1 to 2.
In the remote Arctic, Siberia and Antarctica, it records almost nothing below magnitude 4.
The networks increased during the 16 years. North of 55° N, the yearly counts of magnitude 1–5 in 2017–2025 were approximately 1.6 times the counts in 2010–2015.
Some areas, for example the Kobuk valley, recorded several times as many. Thus, the early years show too few events, and the number of years with events can be too low.
Distances go from the centre of the area. We got the events from 55 degrees to the pole.
For areas at 59 to approximately 59.5° N, the 500 km circle goes a little south of 55° N.
Thus, the detection floor for these areas uses slightly fewer events.

comparisons.title: Solar power on the Moon
paragraphs: A panel that faces the Sun gets 1,361 watts per square metre at all times when the Sun is above the local horizon. There is no atmosphere.
Source: NASA NSSDCA Moon Fact Sheet.

comparisons.title: Sunlit time at Connecting Ridge
paragraphs: Solar power stays at full strength while the Sun is above the horizon. The mean share of time in sunlight for the lunar region is 0.293.
The best 240 m point has a share of 0.935.
At the Sun ceiling of this lunar region, the power on Earth in clear air is 98 watts per square metre.
That is a share of 0.072 of the Moon's power.
Source: NASA Goddard average solar illumination map, PGDA product 69. It uses intervals of 1 hour over 18.6 years on LOLA terrain.

comparisons.title: Sunlit time at Malapert Massif
paragraphs: Solar power stays at full strength while the Sun is above the horizon. The mean share of time in sunlight for the lunar region is 0.359.
The best 240 m point has a share of 0.834.
At the Sun ceiling of this lunar region, the power on Earth in clear air is 265 watts per square metre.
That is a share of 0.195 of the Moon's power.
Source: NASA Goddard average solar illumination map, PGDA product 69. It uses intervals of 1 hour over 18.6 years on LOLA terrain.

paragraphs: Solar power stays at full strength while the Sun is above the horizon. The mean share of time in sunlight for the lunar region is 0.287.
The best 240 m point has a share of 0.788.

comparisons.title: Wind on the Moon
paragraphs: Wind power is 0 watts per square metre. There is no wind or air to carry it.
The fact sheet gives the surface pressure as 3 × 10^−15 bar. The total mass of the atmosphere is 25,000 kg.
Source: NASA NSSDCA Moon Fact Sheet.

comparisons.title: Sunlight at Mars
paragraphs: Above the air, the sunlight is 586.2 watts per square metre, a share of 0.431 of the value for Earth.
During the Mars year, it changes from 490.3 to 713.3 watts per square metre. Source: NASA NSSDCA Mars Fact Sheet.

comparisons.title: Dust at Mars
paragraphs: Dust stays in the sky all year. The optical depth is usually below 1 during the aphelion season, Ls 0–180.
It is more than 3 at the peak of global dust storms. These figures come from observations by 7 landers.
For Earth, the source gives from memory a global mean optical depth of approximately 0.1–0.2 at 550 nm. Nobody checked that figure for Earth.
Source: Space Science Reviews (2017), as recorded in the Mars climate data.

comparisons.title: Air pressure at Mars
paragraphs: The yearly mean pressure in the model is from 480 to 896 Pa at the 57 Mars sites. On Earth at sea level, it is 101,325 Pa.
The lowest value is 480 Pa, at Southern Nectaris Fossae. The highest value is 896 Pa, at McLaughlin crater. The card of each Mars site gives its value.
Source: Mars Climate Database v6.2.

comparisons.title: Wind power at Mars
paragraphs: At the same wind speed, the wind on Mars carries a share of 0.0131 of the wind power on Earth. This share is the ratio of the air densities.
The fact sheets give the air density on Mars as approximately 0.016 ± 0.006 kg per cubic metre. On Earth, it is 1.217 kg per cubic metre.
For the same power, the wind on Mars must be 4.2 times faster.
At 10 m/s, the wind on Mars carries 15 watts per square metre. At sea level on Earth, the wind carries 1,170 watts per square metre.
The pressures from the model give a second value for the density: 0.0117 to 0.0219 kg per cubic metre.
Density = pressure × molar mass / (gas constant × temperature). The second value uses a mean molecular weight of 43.49 and a mean temperature of 214 K.
The winds at the Viking Landers are 2–7 m/s in summer, 5–10 m/s in fall, and 17–30 m/s in dust storms.
Sources: NASA NSSDCA Mars and Earth fact sheets, and the Mars model data for each area.

comparisons.title: Geothermal power on the Moon and Mars
paragraphs: Unknown: not in our data.
